stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OOrI A huge, highly revered golden statue of Genghis Khan is found in Mongolia's Chinggis Khaan National Museum, which opened in October 2022 Image: Chinggis Khaan National Museum Advertisement Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history. The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition " Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols ." The power of a disruptive individual The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project. stories.title: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
stories.summary: The attack on the unidentified victim follows a wave of anti-migrants protests in South Africa this year.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Anti-migrant protesters in South Africa demand that all undocumented foreign nationals leave the country By Ondiro Oganga Published 4 hours ago A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say. According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established. The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg. Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.
